title: The cat
hook: when I play with my cat, who knows if she is playing with me? (Essays 2.12)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was que sais-je: what do I know, Montaigne's motto, held like level scales. Your line was what do I know.

A piece of string dragged slowly across the floor. Under the chair, a cat goes flat, tail twitching. She wiggles, pounces, misses, and looks up at you as if to say that was on purpose. You're the one holding the string, so you're the one running the game. Aren't you? Montaigne had a cat, and somewhere in the same long essay as yesterday's motto, he stops to ask exactly that.
screen: `A STRING ACROSS THE FLOOR.` → `A POUNCE, A MISS.` → `WHO'S RUNNING THE GAME?`

segments.voice: First, the question. When I play with my cat, Montaigne writes, who knows whether she isn't amusing herself with me more than I am with her? It's a light line, and it flips the whole scene. Maybe you're the toy. Second, the silence between us. People and animals don't fully understand each other, he says, and we assume the failure is theirs. But why not ours as much as theirs? It's anybody's guess whose fault it is. By the same reasoning, he adds, they might think of us as the dumb animals. Third, the dog at the crossroads. He passes along a story from the ancient philosopher Chrysippus. A dog, following its master's trail, comes to a place where three roads meet. It sniffs one road. It sniffs a second. Then it runs down the third without sniffing at all, as if it had worked it out: not this one, not that one, so this. Montaigne doesn't wave the story away. He asks why we're so sure the dog wasn't thinking. Fourth, the point underneath. All of this sits in a long argument against human presumption. We're fragile, exposed creatures, he says, and at the same time the proudest, and we hand ourselves the top spot without much evidence. The cat is a gentle example: yesterday's question, what do I know, turned toward the creature on the rug. Who's playing whom is a good question for a pet, and not a bad one for a toddler, a teenager, or a boss.
screen: `MAYBE YOU'RE THE TOY.` · `WHOSE FAULT IS THE SILENCE?` · `THE DOG AT THE CROSSROADS.` · `PRIDE, CUT TO SIZE.` · then, large: `WHO'S PLAYING WHOM?`

segments.voice: If there's an animal near you, a cat, a dog, a bird on a wire, let it be without calling it, and watch where its attention goes, and whether, for a moment, it lands on you. If there's no animal near, remember how one once looked at you. Ask Montaigne's question quietly, what might I look like from there, and rest in not knowing.
The cat. Montaigne, playing with his cat, wonders whether she's playing with him, and asks why the gap between us and animals must be their fault. Today's word.
Your line: who's playing whom. The cat may have her own view of the game. That's day one thousand one hundred sixty.

howItsDone: Readers of Montaigne often remember the cat as a small lesson in humility: when we can't understand another creature, the gap may be ours as much as theirs.

chat.meaning: Montaigne asks who knows whether his cat is amusing herself with him more than he with her, and why the gap between us must be her fault.

Montaigne.meaning: Michel de Montaigne, French nobleman who wrote the Essays

Chrysippus.meaning: ancient Greek philosopher Montaigne cites for the dog story

presumption.meaning: taking more credit to ourselves than we have reason to

sources.ref: Essays 2.12, Apology for Raymond Sebond (when I play with my cat, who knows whether she makes me her pastime more than I make her mine; the defect in communication may be ours as much as theirs; animals may take us for beasts; Chrysippus's dog at the meeting of three roads; presumption as our natural malady)

notes: All Montaigne is paraphrased. The French 'quand je me joue à ma chatte' is from memory of the full sentence ('qui sait si elle passe son temps de moi plus que je ne fais d'elle'); confirm.
Chrysippus's dog: Montaigne attributes it to Chrysippus and says three roads; confirm wording, and that he leaves the question open as the script says.
'We're fragile and at the same time the proudest' paraphrases Montaigne's remark on presumption in 2.12; confirm placement.
